Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: Women in these high-risk groups require different screening regimens than the general population.48,49 Non-modifiable factors associated with increased risk among women eligible for routine screening include increased age;10 at least one first- or second-degree relative with breast cancer;50-52 and heterogeneously or extremely dense breast tissue.53 Women in their 40s with extremely dense breast tissue or at least one first-degree relative with breast cancer are estimated to have a twofold increased risk of breast cancer.50 Additional risk factors that have been associated with an increased risk of breast cancer include use of menopausal hormone therapy, increasing body mass index (BMI), alcohol use, and nulliparity or giving birth after age 35.54 Risk factors associated with a decreased risk of breast cancer include breastfeeding and increased physical activity.54 Breast density is a radiographic measure of breast tissue that is associated with increased risk for breast cancer and reduced mammography sensitivity [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. A large cohort study from the United States highlights the potential importance of including additional risk factors to inform supplemental screening strategies and reduce false-positive rates [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 15]. Treatment or Intervention Breast cancer treatment regimens are highly individualized according to each patient’s clinical status, cancer stage, tumor biomarkers, clinical subtype, and personal preferences [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3]. Noninvasive (in-situ) lesions are contained in the ductal-lobular unit and do not extend into the basement membrane or surrounding tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: Women in these high-risk groups require different screening regimens than the general population.48,49 Non-modifiable factors associated with increased risk among women eligible for routine screening include increased age;10 at least one first- or second-degree relative with breast cancer;50-52 and heterogeneously or extremely dense breast tissue.53 Women in their 40s with extremely dense breast tissue or at least one first-degree relative with breast cancer are estimated to have a twofold increased risk of breast cancer.50 Additional risk factors that have been associated with an increased risk of breast cancer include use of menopausal hormone therapy, increasing body mass index (BMI), alcohol use, and nulliparity or giving birth after age 35.54 Risk factors associated with a decreased risk of breast cancer include breastfeeding and increased physical activity.54 Breast density is a radiographic measure of breast tissue that is associated with increased risk for breast cancer and reduced mammography sensitivity [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. A large cohort study from the United States highlights the potential importance of including additional risk factors to inform supplemental screening strategies and reduce false-positive rates [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. The highest rates of advanced cancer were seen in women with heterogeneously dense or extremely dense breasts and at least 2.5 percent 5-year risk of breast cancer calculated using the BCSC risk calculator (described below) [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 16]. Treatment or Intervention Breast cancer treatment regimens are highly individualized according to each patient’s clinical status, cancer stage, tumor biomarkers, clinical subtype, and personal preferences [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3]. Noninvasive (in-situ) lesions are contained in the ductal-lobular unit and do not extend into the basement membrane or surrounding tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

Introduction, Page: 14]. A large cohort study from the United States highlights the potential importance of including additional risk factors to inform supplemental screening strategies and reduce false-positive rates [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Treatment or Intervention Breast cancer treatment regimens are highly individualized according to each patient’s clinical status, cancer stage, tumor biomarkers, clinical subtype, and personal preferences [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3]. Noninvasive (in-situ) lesions are contained in the ductal-lobular unit and do not extend into the basement membrane or surrounding tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

A large cohort study from the United States highlights the potential importance of including additional risk factors to inform supplemental screening strategies and reduce false-positive rates [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. final_answer:
Common anatomical (histologic) types of breast cancer include:

- **Invasive ductal carcinoma** (the most common invasive type) [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  
- **Invasive lobular carcinoma** (grows more slowly and is less common than ductal carcinoma) [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  
- **Inflammatory breast cancer** (a rare form that blocks lymph vessels in the skin of the breast) [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  
- **Carcinoma in situ** (abnormal cells confined to the ducts or lobules without invasion) [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 2-3]  
- **Metastatic (stage 4) breast cancer** (breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body) [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  

Common molecular (biomarker‑based) subtypes of breast cancer include:

- **Hormone‑receptor (HR) positive / HER2‑negative** (often called luminal A tumors, representing about 73 % of invasive cancers) [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 13]  
- **Luminal B** (HR positive but with higher proliferation or HER2 overexpression) [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Molecular subtypes of breast cancer, Page: 4-5]  
- **HER2‑positive** (overexpression of the HER2 protein) [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Molecular subtypes of breast cancer, Page: 4-5]  
- **Triple‑negative** (lacking HR receptors and HER2) [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Molecular subtypes of breast cancer, Page: 4-5]  

These anatomical and molecular classifications help guide prognosis and treatment decisions.

Treatment or Intervention Breast cancer treatment regimens are highly individualized according to each patient’s clinical status, cancer stage, tumor biomarkers, clinical subtype, and personal preferences [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3]. Noninvasive (in-situ) lesions are contained in the ductal-lobular unit and do not extend into the basement membrane or surrounding tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: Women in these high-risk groups require different screening regimens than the general population.48,49 Non-modifiable factors associated with increased risk among women eligible for routine screening include increased age;10 at least one first- or second-degree relative with breast cancer;50-52 and heterogeneously or extremely dense breast tissue.53 Women in their 40s with extremely dense breast tissue or at least one first-degree relative with breast cancer are estimated to have a twofold increased risk of breast cancer.50 Additional risk factors that have been associated with an increased risk of breast cancer include use of menopausal hormone therapy, increasing body mass index (BMI), alcohol use, and nulliparity or giving birth after age 35.54 Risk factors associated with a decreased risk of breast cancer include breastfeeding and increased physical activity.54 Breast density is a radiographic measure of breast tissue that is associated with increased risk for breast cancer and reduced mammography sensitivity [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. A large cohort study from the United States highlights the potential importance of including additional risk factors to inform supplemental screening strategies and reduce false-positive rates [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 15]. The highest rates of advanced cancer were seen in women with heterogeneously dense or extremely dense breasts and at least 2.5 percent 5-year risk of breast cancer calculated using the BCSC risk calculator (described below) [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 16]. It describes the amount and distribution of dense fibrous and glandular tissue relative to surrounding fat tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. final_answer: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a precancerous condition in which abnormal cells are found in the lining of a breast duct [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Research Results, Page: 59]. DCIS is also referred to as noninvasive breast cancer, intraductal carcinoma, or stage 0 breast cancer [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 4]. It is a noninvasive condition with abnormal cells in the breast duct lining, and it has varying clinical behavior and pathologic characteristics [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. DCIS is considered a precursor lesion for invasive ductal carcinoma and accounts for approximately 20 to 25 percent of all breast neoplasms, with its incidence increasing due to the widespread use of mammographic screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11].

final_answer:
Breast cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the breast and can affect one or both breasts. It occurs when cells in the breast grow without control, forming a mass called a tumor, which may spread to other parts of the body [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 1].

Breast cancer can develop in different types of breast tissue, including:
- Glandular tissue, which includes milk glands, milk ducts, and lobules. Most breast cancers are ductal cancers, which start in the ducts.
- Fibrous and fatty tissue (stroma), which can give rise to a type of tumor called a phyllodes tumor.
- The nipple, where a rare type of cancer called Paget disease of the breast can start.
- Blood vessels and lymph vessels, where inflammatory breast cancer and angiosarcoma can develop [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 1-3].

The development of breast cancer is a multistep process involving the accumulation of genetic alterations and the influence of various risk factors. Initially, cells may undergo ductal hyperplasia without atypia. Over time, these cells can accumulate mutations and genomic instabilities, leading to precursor lesions. These lesions can evolve into in situ carcinoma, where the cancer cells are confined within the ducts but have not yet invaded surrounding tissues. If the cancer progresses further, it can become invasive, spreading into surrounding breast tissue and potentially to nearby lymph nodes or other organs [Source: Nature Review Breast cancer pathogenesis and treatments (2025).pdf, Page: 3].

final_answer:
The common anatomical types of breast cancer include:

- **Invasive ductal carcinoma**: This type begins in the cells that line the milk ducts and has spread beyond where it first formed. It is the most common breast cancer diagnosis [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].
- **Invasive lobular carcinoma**: This type begins in the cells that line the breast glands that make milk, called lobules, and has spread beyond where it first formed. It grows more slowly and is less common than invasive ductal carcinoma. Lobular carcinoma is more often found in both breasts than are other types of breast cancer [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].
- **Inflammatory breast cancer**: This is a rare form of breast cancer in which cancer cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the breast. The affected breast often looks swollen and red, or inflamed [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].
- **Triple-negative breast cancer**: This form of breast cancer lacks hormone receptors and the protein called human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). It has a higher risk of recurrence than most other forms of breast cancer [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].
- **Metastatic breast cancer**: Also called stage 4 breast cancer, this type has spread from the breast to another part of the body [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].

The common molecular subtypes of breast cancer are defined by the presence or absence of hormone receptors and the HER2 protein. These include:

- **Hormone receptor (HR) positive**: This subtype includes cancers that have receptors for estrogen (ER) or progesterone (PR). The most common subtype is HR+/HER2-, also known as Luminal A tumors, which represent nearly three-quarters of invasive breast cancers (73%). These tumors are usually less aggressive and responsive to hormone therapy, resulting in a better prognosis [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 13].
- **HER2-positive**: This subtype includes cancers that have an excess of the HER2 protein. These cancers tend to be more aggressive but can be treated with targeted therapies [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Molecular subtypes of breast cancer, Page: 4-5].
- **Triple-negative breast cancer**: This subtype lacks receptors for estrogen, progesterone, and HER2. It is more aggressive and has a higher risk of recurrence [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].

Understanding the specific type and molecular subtype of breast cancer is crucial for planning the best treatment approach [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 2-3].

final_answer:
Breast cancer is caused by certain changes in how breast cells function, especially how they grow and divide into new cells [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Causes and Risk Factors, Page: 5]. 

The primary risk factors for breast cancer include:
- Increasing age, which is the most important risk factor besides female biological sex [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Causes and Risk Factors, Page: 5].
- Personal health history, such as having had breast cancer in the past, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), or exposure to high levels of radiation, particularly at a young age [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
- Having a history of certain kinds of breast changes, such as dense breasts, which not only increases the risk of breast cancer but also makes it more difficult to detect on mammograms [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
- Excess body weight, especially after menopause [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
- Taking combination (estrogen plus progestin) hormone replacement therapy for symptoms of menopause [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
- Exposure to DES (a synthetic estrogen) before birth (in utero) or during pregnancy [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
- Lifestyle factors such as poor dietary habits, alcohol intake, and sedentary lifestyles, which are particularly prevalent in high-income countries [Source: Frntiers Breast Cancer pathogenesis, diagnosis and treatment (2026).pdf, Section: 2.3 Lifestyle factors, Page: 4].

It is important to note that having one or more of these risk factors does not mean that you will get breast cancer, and some people who get breast cancer do not have known risk factors [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Causes and Risk Factors, Page: 5]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer:
Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a noninvasive condition where abnormal cells are found in the lining of a breast duct [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 4]. It is also referred to as noninvasive breast cancer, intraductal carcinoma, or stage 0 breast cancer [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 4]. DCIS is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. It accounts for approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms diagnosed in the United States [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. DCIS is heterogenous and has varying clinical behavior and pathologic characteristics, with some forms viewed as precursor lesions for invasive ductal carcinoma [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. 

Women diagnosed with DCIS have a substantial risk of overdiagnosis and overtreatment because there is currently no way to tell which lesions found on screening mammograms will progress to invasive disease [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Research Results, Page: 59]. Treatment for DCIS, which may include surgery, radiation, and endocrine treatment, is generally intended to reduce the risk for future invasive breast cancer [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3]. However, the natural history of screen-detected DCIS is unclear in terms of the percentage of cases that would have progressed to invasive cancer in the absence of treatment [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14].

final_answer:
The potential harms of breast cancer screening include:

- **False-positive results**: These can cause mental and emotional distress and require additional follow-up procedures, such as biopsies, which can themselves cause harm. False-positive results are more common among younger women, women with dense breasts, women who have had previous breast biopsies, women with a family history of breast cancer, and women who are taking estrogen (for example, menopausal hormone therapy) [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Screening, Page: 13-14].
- **Overdiagnosis and overtreatment**: Some cancers found during screening may not have caused problems during a woman’s lifetime and would not have needed treatment. Finding these cancers earlier may not improve someone’s health or help them live longer but will expose them to the harms of treatment [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Screening, Page: 13-14].
- **Delayed diagnosis**: Diagnosis can be delayed due to false-negative results. False-negative results are more common among women with dense breasts. Diagnosis can also be delayed if someone with a recent normal screening test result does not check with their doctor about symptoms that could be from an interval breast cancer [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Screening, Page: 13-14].
- **Radiation exposure**: Radiation from mammography can potentially cause cancer, although the risk is very low [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Screening, Page: 13-14].

Additionally, the potential harms of breast cancer screening include:

- **False-positive results and additional testing**: These can lead to psychological harms, additional testing, and invasive diagnostic follow-up procedures (e.g., biopsy) [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 17].
- **Overdiagnosis and overtreatment**: These are harms from the detection, diagnosis, and treatment of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or invasive cancers that would not have led to health problems without detection [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 17].
- **Increased radiation exposure**: DBT screening has been associated with an increased risk for breast biopsy compared with conventional DM and higher radiation exposure when performed in conjunction with conventional DM, which has been estimated to be as much as two times greater than that associated with DM (with women with dense breasts exposed to even higher doses) [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 17].
- **Supplemental screening in women with dense breasts**: This may include additional false-positive recall and biopsies when compared with standard screening mammography [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 17].

It is important to discuss these potential harms with a qualified healthcare professional to make an informed decision about breast cancer screening.

final_answer:
The USPSTF concludes that the evidence is insufficient to determine the balance of benefits and harms of supplemental screening for breast cancer with breast ultrasound or MRI, regardless of breast density [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Importance, Page: 2]. Specifically, the USPSTF found insufficient evidence on the effects of supplemental screening on health outcomes, and no studies of supplemental screening reported on health outcomes or on the incidence of and progression to advanced breast cancer over more than one round of screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Screening Interval, Page: 9].

The USPSTF's I statement means that there is insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms, or to recommend for or against supplemental screening, and that women should talk with their clinicians about what is best given their individual circumstances [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Disparities in Breast Cancer Outcomes, Page: 4].

The USPSTF also calls for more research to help close this important evidence gap [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Screening Interval, Page: 9]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer:
The current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening mammography in women 75 years or older [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Summary of Recommendations, Page: 1]. 

Breast cancer incidence remains high in women aged 75 years or older, with rates of 453.3 and 409.9 cases per 100,000 women aged 75 to 79 and 80 to 84 years, respectively [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Potential Preventable Burden, Page: 5]. However, no randomized clinical trials (RCTs) of breast cancer screening have included women 75 years or older [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Potential Preventable Burden, Page: 5]. 

Collaborative modeling suggests that screening in women 75 years or older may be beneficial, but a trial emulation found no benefit with breast cancer screening in women aged 75 to 84 years [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Potential Preventable Burden, Page: 5]. 

Therefore, the USPSTF concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against screening mammography in women 75 years or older [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Summary of Recommendations, Page: 1]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

Introduction, Page: 14]. A large cohort study from the United States highlights the potential importance of including additional risk factors to inform supplemental screening strategies and reduce false-positive rates [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. final_answer:
Breast cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the breast. It can develop in one or both breasts and occurs when cells in the breast grow without control, forming a mass called a tumor that may spread to other parts of the body [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 1].

Breast cancer can form in different parts of the breast, including:
- Glandular tissue, which includes milk glands, milk ducts, and lobules. Cancers that start in the ducts are called ductal cancers, and those that start in the lobules are called lobular cancers. Most breast cancers are ductal cancers.
- Fibrous tissue and fatty tissue (stroma), which fill the spaces between the lobules and ducts and give the breast its shape and size. A type of breast tumor called a phyllodes tumor can start in the stroma.
- The nipple, where a type of breast cancer called Paget disease of the breast can start.
- Blood vessels and lymph vessels, where inflammatory breast cancer and angiosarcoma can occur [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 1-3].

The development of breast cancer is a multistep process involving the accumulation of genetic alterations and the influence of various risk factors. Initially, cells may undergo ductal hyperplasia without atypia. Over time, with the promotion phase, mutations accumulate, leading to the expansion of mutation clones. These cells may produce autocrine growth factors or recruit inflammatory and stromal cells to produce these factors, evolving mechanisms to evade the immune system. This process results in precursor lesions, such as ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), where the pathological cells are confined within the ducts but have not yet invaded surrounding tissues. As the disease progresses, cells acquire invasive and metastatic properties, facilitated by genetic alterations and interactions with the tumor microenvironment, leading to invasive breast cancer [Source: Nature Review Breast cancer pathogenesis and treatments (2025).pdf, Page: 3].

Invasive breast cancer can spread into surrounding breast tissue and can also spread to nearby lymph nodes or other organs throughout the body [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 2-3]. Early detection and interventions are crucial to managing breast cancer effectively [Source: Nature Review Breast cancer pathogenesis and treatments (2025).pdf, Page: 3].

final_answer:
The common anatomical types of breast cancer include:

- **Invasive ductal carcinoma**: This type begins in the cells that line the milk ducts and has spread beyond where it first formed. It is the most common breast cancer diagnosis [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].
- **Invasive lobular carcinoma**: This type begins in the cells that line the breast glands that make milk, called lobules, and has spread beyond where it first formed. It grows more slowly and is less common than invasive ductal carcinoma [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].
- **Inflammatory breast cancer**: This is a rare form of breast cancer in which cancer cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the breast. It is called inflammatory because the affected breast often looks swollen and red, or inflamed [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].
- **Triple-negative breast cancer**: This form of breast cancer lacks hormone receptors and the HER2 protein. It has a higher risk of recurrence than most other forms of breast cancer [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].
- **Metastatic breast cancer**: Also called stage 4 breast cancer, this type has spread from the breast to another part of the body [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].

The common molecular subtypes of breast cancer are defined by the presence or absence of hormone receptors and the HER2 protein. These include:

- **Hormone receptor (HR) positive**: These cancers have receptors for estrogen (ER) and/or progesterone (PR). The most common subtype is HR+/HER2-, also known as Luminal A tumors, which represent nearly three-quarters of invasive breast cancers (73%). These tumors are usually less aggressive and responsive to hormone therapy, resulting in a better prognosis [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 13].
- **HER2-positive**: These cancers have an excess of the HER2 protein. They tend to be more aggressive but can be treated with targeted therapies [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Molecular subtypes of breast cancer, Page: 4-5].
- **Triple-negative breast cancer**: This subtype lacks receptors for estrogen, progesterone, and HER2. It is more aggressive and has a higher risk of recurrence [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3].

For more detailed information on these subtypes and their implications for treatment, you should consult with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer:
Breast cancer is caused by certain changes in how breast cells function, particularly in how they grow and divide into new cells [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Causes and Risk Factors, Page: 5]. 

The primary risk factors for breast cancer include:

1. **Increasing Age**: The most important risk factor for breast cancer, besides female biological sex, is increasing age [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Causes and Risk Factors, Page: 5].
2. **Personal Health History and Breast Conditions**:
   - Having had breast cancer in the past [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
   - Having had ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) in the past [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
   - Having been exposed to high levels of radiation in the past, particularly at a young age, such as during treatment for childhood cancer [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
   - Having a history of certain kinds of breast changes [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
   - Having dense breasts, which not only increases the risk of breast cancer but also makes it more difficult to detect breast cancer on mammograms [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
3. **Family History and Genetics**:
   - Having at least one first- or second-degree relative with breast cancer [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14].
4. **Lifestyle Factors**:
   - Excess body weight, especially after menopause [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
   - Taking combination (estrogen plus progestin) hormone replacement therapy for symptoms of menopause [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
   - Drinking alcohol [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
   - Sedentary lifestyle and poor dietary habits, such as consuming fast food and sugary foods, which are more prevalent in high-income countries [Source: Frntiers Breast Cancer pathogenesis, diagnosis and treatment (2026).pdf, Section: 2.3 Lifestyle factors, Page: 4].
5. **Other Factors**:
   - Having been exposed to DES (a synthetic estrogen) before birth (in utero) or having taken it during pregnancy [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Personal health history and breast conditions, Page: 5-6].
   - Nulliparity or giving birth after age 35 [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14].

It is important to note that having one or more of these risk factors does not mean that you will get breast cancer, and some people who get breast cancer do not have known risk factors [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Causes and Risk Factors, Page: 5]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a noninvasive condition where abnormal cells are found in the lining of a breast duct [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 4]. It is also referred to as noninvasive breast cancer, intraductal carcinoma, or stage 0 breast cancer [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 4]. DCIS is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography and accounts for approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms diagnosed in the United States [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. The clinical behavior and pathologic characteristics of DCIS are heterogeneous, and some forms are viewed as precursor lesions for invasive ductal carcinoma [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Women diagnosed with DCIS have a substantial risk of overdiagnosis and overtreatment because there is currently no way to tell which lesions found on screening mammograms will progress to invasive disease [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Research Results, Page: 59]. Treatment for DCIS is generally recommended and may include surgery, radiation, and endocrine treatment, aimed at reducing the risk of future invasive breast cancer [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3].

final_answer:
Breast cancer is a disease that begins in the breast and can involve one or both breasts. It occurs when breast cells grow without control, forming a mass called a tumor that may spread to other parts of the body. The condition most commonly affects females aged 45 years and older, but anyone with breasts can develop it, and it is rare in children and males. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 1]

The cancer can arise in several tissue types: glandular tissue (including milk ducts and lobules, with ductal cancers being the most common), fibrous and fatty stroma, the nipple (e.g., Paget disease), or the lining of blood and lymph vessels (e.g., inflammatory breast cancer and angiosarcoma). Most breast cancers are ductal cancers. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 1]

When abnormal cells are confined to the ducts or lobules and have not spread, the disease is called carcinoma in situ; when the cells have invaded surrounding breast tissue and may spread to lymph nodes or other organs, it is invasive cancer. The majority of breast cancers are invasive. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 1]

Globally, breast cancer is one of the most frequently diagnosed malignancies among women, with about 20 million new cases and 9.7 million deaths estimated worldwide (GLOBOCAN 2022). Approximately one out of seven women will develop breast cancer during her lifetime, and early‑stage, non‑metastatic disease has a 70–80 % chance of cure when detected early. [Source: Frntiers Breast Cancer pathogenesis, diagnosis and treatment (2026).pdf, Section: 1 Introduction, Page: 2]

- **Inflammatory breast cancer** – a rare form in which cancer cells block lymph vessels in the breast skin, often presenting with swelling and redness. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  
- **Triple‑negative breast cancer** – lacks hormone receptors and HER2 protein, and has a higher risk of recurrence than most other types. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]

final_answer:
I’m not a medical professional, but the most recent USPSTF guidance for women who are 75 years or older states that the evidence is **insufficient to determine whether the benefits of routine screening mammography outweigh the harms** in this age group. The USPSTF therefore does **not** make a recommendation for or against screening in women 75 years or older. [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Disparities in Breast Cancer Outcomes, Page: 4]  

Because no randomized trials have enrolled women 75 years or older, the evidence base is limited. Modeling studies suggest a possible benefit, but an emulated trial found no benefit for screening women 75–84 years. [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Potential Preventable Burden, Page: 5]  

The USPSTF also notes that there is insufficient evidence to recommend supplemental screening (ultrasound or MRI) for women with dense breasts who have a normal mammogram. [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Disparities in Breast Cancer Outcomes, Page: 4]  

Given these uncertainties, clinicians are encouraged to use their clinical judgment and discuss the potential risks and benefits with you, taking into account your overall health, life expectancy, personal preferences, and any other risk factors. [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Disparities in Breast Cancer Outcomes, Page: 4]  

If you are considering screening, it would be helpful to have a shared‑decision‑making conversation with your healthcare provider to weigh the possible benefits, harms, and your individual circumstances.

Noninvasive (in-situ) lesions are contained in the ductal-lobular unit and do not extend into the basement membrane or surrounding tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: Potential harms of screening for breast cancer include false-positive and false-negative results, need for additional imaging and biopsy, overdiagnosis, and radiation exposure [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Screening Interval, Page: 7]. These include two RCTs in the United States (COMET)265 and United Kingdom (LORIS)266 and a patient preference trial in The Netherlands (LORD).267 Until these trials are complete (estimated 2029– 2030), the effectiveness of treatment of screen-detected DCIS to reduce breast cancer mortality remains unclear, and the extent to which it represents overdiagnosis and overtreatment is unknown.124 Treatment harms are of greatest concern when occurring among people who would not have otherwise experienced negative health consequences had their cancer not been screen-detected and treated [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 4. Discussion, Page: 69]. The potential harms of breast cancer screening include: False-positive results [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Screening, Page: 13-14]. Combined with the similar cancer detection results for DBT and DM, the findings on interval cancer additionally suggest similar screening effectiveness for the two technologies based on the available evidence [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 4. Discussion, Page: 55]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer:
I’m not aware of any evidence‑based breast‑cancer screening recommendations that apply to men, including men who are 75 years old. The USPSTF and other guideline bodies focus on women and persons assigned female at birth, and they explicitly state that their recommendations do not apply to men. [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Disparities in Breast Cancer Outcomes, Page: 4]  

For women who are 75 years or older, the USPSTF notes that the evidence is insufficient to determine whether screening mammography is beneficial or harmful, and therefore they issue an “I statement” (insufficient evidence). [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Disparities in Breast Cancer Outcomes, Page: 4]  

Because the guidelines do not cover men, there is no recommendation for routine breast‑cancer screening in a 75‑year‑old man. It is best to discuss any concerns or risk factors with a qualified healthcare professional, who can consider your overall health, family history, and any other relevant factors.

Treatment or Intervention Breast cancer treatment regimens are highly individualized according to each patient’s clinical status, cancer stage, tumor biomarkers, clinical subtype, and personal preferences [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3]. Noninvasive (in-situ) lesions are contained in the ductal-lobular unit and do not extend into the basement membrane or surrounding tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: The American Cancer Society recommends that women with an average risk of breast cancer should undergo regular screening mammography starting at age 45 years [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Recommendations of Others, Page: 10]. The American College of Radiology also recommends breast cancer risk assessment by age 25 years for all individuals [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Recommendations of Others, Page: 10]. Based on self-reported Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data from 2020, 78 percent of all women ages 50 to 74 reported having a mammography in the past two years [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 4. Discussion, Page: 61]. No eligible studies were identified that reported on the potential harms of personalized screening programs using risk assessment [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Summary of Results, Page: 43]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: Ductal Carcinoma In Situ Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a precancerous condition in which abnormal cells are found in the lining of a breast duct [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Research Results, Page: 59]. Treatment or Intervention Breast cancer treatment regimens are highly individualized according to each patient’s clinical status, cancer stage, tumor biomarkers, clinical subtype, and personal preferences [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3]. Noninvasive (in-situ) lesions are contained in the ductal-lobular unit and do not extend into the basement membrane or surrounding tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: Women in these high-risk groups require different screening regimens than the general population.48,49 Non-modifiable factors associated with increased risk among women eligible for routine screening include increased age;10 at least one first- or second-degree relative with breast cancer;50-52 and heterogeneously or extremely dense breast tissue.53 Women in their 40s with extremely dense breast tissue or at least one first-degree relative with breast cancer are estimated to have a twofold increased risk of breast cancer.50 Additional risk factors that have been associated with an increased risk of breast cancer include use of menopausal hormone therapy, increasing body mass index (BMI), alcohol use, and nulliparity or giving birth after age 35.54 Risk factors associated with a decreased risk of breast cancer include breastfeeding and increased physical activity.54 Breast density is a radiographic measure of breast tissue that is associated with increased risk for breast cancer and reduced mammography sensitivity [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. A large cohort study from the United States highlights the potential importance of including additional risk factors to inform supplemental screening strategies and reduce false-positive rates [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 16]. These include two RCTs in the United States (COMET)265 and United Kingdom (LORIS)266 and a patient preference trial in The Netherlands (LORD).267 Until these trials are complete (estimated 2029– 2030), the effectiveness of treatment of screen-detected DCIS to reduce breast cancer mortality remains unclear, and the extent to which it represents overdiagnosis and overtreatment is unknown.124 Treatment harms are of greatest concern when occurring among people who would not have otherwise experienced negative health consequences had their cancer not been screen-detected and treated [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 4. Discussion, Page: 69]. The potential harms of breast cancer screening include: False-positive results [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Screening, Page: 13-14]. final_answer:
Breast cancer can arise in several distinct histologic and clinical forms. The most commonly referenced types are:

- **Invasive ductal carcinoma** – the most common diagnosis, beginning in the cells lining the milk ducts and spreading beyond the original site. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  
- **Invasive lobular carcinoma** – begins in the cells lining the breast lobules, grows more slowly, and is less common than ductal carcinoma. It is often found in both breasts. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  
- **Inflammatory breast cancer** – a rare form in which cancer cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the breast, producing a swollen, red appearance and a high risk of recurrence. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  
- **Triple‑negative breast cancer** – lacks hormone receptors (ER/PR) and HER2, and has a higher risk of recurrence than most other forms. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  
- **Metastatic (stage IV) breast cancer** – cancer that has spread from the breast to other parts of the body via lymph or blood. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Types of Breast Cancer, Page: 3]  
- **Carcinoma in situ** – abnormal cells confined to the lobules or ducts that have not yet invaded surrounding tissue. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 2-3]  
- **Phyllodes tumor** – a tumor that can arise in the breast stroma (fibrous and fatty tissue). [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 1]  
- **Paget disease of the breast** – a cancer that starts in the nipple. [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: What Is Breast Cancer?, Page: 1]  

These categories reflect the main histologic and clinical distinctions used to guide diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis. Individual screening and treatment decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

Treatment or Intervention Breast cancer treatment regimens are highly individualized according to each patient’s clinical status, cancer stage, tumor biomarkers, clinical subtype, and personal preferences [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3]. Noninvasive (in-situ) lesions are contained in the ductal-lobular unit and do not extend into the basement membrane or surrounding tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: The American Cancer Society recommends that women with an average risk of breast cancer should undergo regular screening mammography starting at age 45 years [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Recommendations of Others, Page: 10]. The American College of Radiology also recommends breast cancer risk assessment by age 25 years for all individuals [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Recommendations of Others, Page: 10]. Based on self-reported Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data from 2020, 78 percent of all women ages 50 to 74 reported having a mammography in the past two years [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 4. Discussion, Page: 61]. No eligible studies were identified that reported on the potential harms of personalized screening programs using risk assessment [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Summary of Results, Page: 43]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

Introduction, Page: 15]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

final_answer: Women in these high-risk groups require different screening regimens than the general population.48,49 Non-modifiable factors associated with increased risk among women eligible for routine screening include increased age;10 at least one first- or second-degree relative with breast cancer;50-52 and heterogeneously or extremely dense breast tissue.53 Women in their 40s with extremely dense breast tissue or at least one first-degree relative with breast cancer are estimated to have a twofold increased risk of breast cancer.50 Additional risk factors that have been associated with an increased risk of breast cancer include use of menopausal hormone therapy, increasing body mass index (BMI), alcohol use, and nulliparity or giving birth after age 35.54 Risk factors associated with a decreased risk of breast cancer include breastfeeding and increased physical activity.54 Breast density is a radiographic measure of breast tissue that is associated with increased risk for breast cancer and reduced mammography sensitivity [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. A large cohort study from the United States highlights the potential importance of including additional risk factors to inform supplemental screening strategies and reduce false-positive rates [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 15]. The highest rates of advanced cancer were seen in women with heterogeneously dense or extremely dense breasts and at least 2.5 percent 5-year risk of breast cancer calculated using the BCSC risk calculator (described below) [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 16]. It describes the amount and distribution of dense fibrous and glandular tissue relative to surrounding fat tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. These include two RCTs in the United States (COMET)265 and United Kingdom (LORIS)266 and a patient preference trial in The Netherlands (LORD).267 Until these trials are complete (estimated 2029– 2030), the effectiveness of treatment of screen-detected DCIS to reduce breast cancer mortality remains unclear, and the extent to which it represents overdiagnosis and overtreatment is unknown.124 Treatment harms are of greatest concern when occurring among people who would not have otherwise experienced negative health consequences had their cancer not been screen-detected and treated [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 4. Discussion, Page: 69]. The potential harms of breast cancer screening include: False-positive results [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Screening, Page: 13-14]. Combined with the similar cancer detection results for DBT and DM, the findings on interval cancer additionally suggest similar screening effectiveness for the two technologies based on the available evidence [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 4. final_answer: Ductal Carcinoma In Situ Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a precancerous condition in which abnormal cells are found in the lining of a breast duct [Source: NCINIH – Breast Cancer Overview (Patient & Professional Versions).pdf, Section: Breast Cancer Research Results, Page: 59]. Treatment or Intervention Breast cancer treatment regimens are highly individualized according to each patient’s clinical status, cancer stage, tumor biomarkers, clinical subtype, and personal preferences [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Treatment or Intervention, Page: 3]. Noninvasive (in-situ) lesions are contained in the ductal-lobular unit and do not extend into the basement membrane or surrounding tissue [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 11]. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common noninvasive breast condition detected with mammography.14 Approximately 16 percent of breast neoplasms (invasive cancer and in situ conditions) diagnosed in the United States are DCIS.32 Most DCIS cases are diagnosed with breast imaging, owing to the widespread use of screening mammography and its ability to identify microcalcifications.39,40 Older studies of palpable DCIS lesions indicated that 14 to 53 percent of untreated DCIS progress to invasive cancer over 8 to 22 years.41 These studies may have limited applicability, however, since the natural history of screen-detected lesions would likely differ from clinically presenting cancers, and represent the majority of DCIS cases in the current era of widespread mammography screening [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 1. Introduction, Page: 14]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

The American College of Radiology also recommends breast cancer risk assessment by age 25 years for all individuals [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-rec.pdf, Section: Recommendations of Others, Page: 10]. Based on self-reported Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data from 2020, 78 percent of all women ages 50 to 74 reported having a mammography in the past two years [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Chapter 4. Discussion, Page: 61]. No eligible studies were identified that reported on the potential harms of personalized screening programs using risk assessment [Source: breast-cancer-screening-final-evidence-review.pdf, Section: Summary of Results, Page: 43]. Individual screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

Discussion, Page: 69].
